parts.title: Growth Now, Profit Later: When the Startup Race Makes Sense
parts.part1:
For some startups, profit is not the first finish line.

They spend heavily to gain users, enter markets, and grow faster than competitors. This can look dangerous. But when a company has a real network effect, speed may have a clear economic purpose.

Research by Michael Katz and Carl Shapiro in 1985 explained the basic idea. A product may become more valuable to each user as more people use it.

That can start a powerful cycle.

More users create more value. More value attracts more users. An early lead may then build into a lasting advantage. In these markets, even the product with the best technology does not always win. Starting late can become a growing problem.
parts.part2:
Pete Flint of NFX argued in 2020 that companies with genuine network effects may have good reasons to choose growth before profit. Some markets can become “winner-take-most” races. After reaching critical mass, a company may also have a chance to move from losses to profit.

But there is a trap hidden inside the word “growth.”

A rising customer count does not prove that a strong network is forming. NFX presents Groupon as a warning. Its fast expansion hid the loss of merchants and sellers that could not be sustained.

The article also points to some direct-to-consumer companies in mattresses, shoes, and meal kits. They used blitzscaling-style growth without strong network effects or other clear defenses. Several later faced lower-value funding rounds and investor losses.

In other words, speed can build a fortress—or simply make a weak business burn money faster.
parts.point_one_body: NFX suggests annual growth of three to five times after product-market fit at the Seed or Series A stage. Later, growth should work together with efficient customer acquisition. Useful checks include the Rule of 40 and recovering customer acquisition costs within about three to six months.
parts.point_two_heading: The market is asking harder questions
parts.point_two_body: NFX notes that private equity acquisitions rose from 4% of relevant transactions in 2008 to 11% in 2019. This does not prove a complete return to profit, but it signals greater interest in efficiency. A 2020 *Business Horizons* paper by Kuratko, Holt, and Neubert also critically examined blitzscaling.
parts.in_one_line: “Growth before profit makes sense when every new user strengthens the business. Without that engine, speed may only help the problems arrive sooner.”

parts.title: The User Rush: Why Some Startups Choose Speed Before Profit
parts.part1:
At first, the plan sounds strange: lose money now, grow fast, and think about profit later.

But for some startups, user growth can change the product itself. This happens when a business has a network effect.

Think of a service that helps people connect. When more people join, the service can become more useful for each person. Katz and Shapiro explained this idea as “network externalities” in their 1985 work.

Then a powerful circle can begin.

More users create more value. More value attracts more users.

An early lead can build on itself and become a lasting advantage. A late start can also become a bigger problem over time. In such a market, even the product with the best technology may not win.

This is why speed can be a rational choice. Pete Flint of NFX wrote in 2020 that a company with a true network effect may first run at a loss. It tries to reach a large enough network before rivals do. After that, it may be able to move into profit.
parts.part2:
But this logic has a clear limit.

Growth is not magic. If each new customer does not make the product stronger, fast spending may only make a weak business larger. Easy money can also hide problems and reduce the pressure to become efficient.

NFX therefore suggests changing the goal as a startup grows. Once people clearly want the product, a Seed or Series A company may aim to grow three to five times in one year. At Series B or C, growth should come with efficient ways to get customers. Later, the company should move toward profit.

In 2020, Kuratko, Holt, and Neubert also examined blitzscaling in the peer-reviewed journal *Business Horizons*. Blitzscaling means choosing very fast growth over efficiency. The real question is not simply, “Can we grow fast?” It is, “Does speed create a lasting advantage?”
parts.point_one_body: NFX uses Groupon as a warning. Its fast expansion hid a serious problem: merchants and sellers were leaving. NFX also discusses some mattress, shoe, and meal-kit companies. They chased blitzscaling without network effects or another strong defense. The article links these cases to down rounds and investor losses.
parts.point_two_heading: Growth must pass a health check
parts.point_two_body: Investors also watch efficiency. NFX gives the Rule of 40: revenue growth plus profit margin should total more than 40%. It also says customer costs should come back within three to six months. Private-equity acquisitions rose from 4% of relevant deals in 2008 to 11% in 2019. NFX presents this as part of a wider return to efficiency.
parts.in_one_line: Growth before profit makes sense when every new user strengthens the business. Without that engine, speed can turn hidden weakness into a larger and more expensive problem.
